meta.title: Shikhi Digital — we grade the thinking, not the answer
meta.description: Shikhi Digital is a learning platform for children aged 8 to 13 that grades how they reason, not just whether their answer was right.

hero.sub: Your child explains why they chose what they chose. We read the reasoning — with the correct answer deliberately hidden from the grader — and send you one honest page every Sunday.
hero.trust: No child logins. No ads. Nothing your child writes is ever indexed.

proof.kicker: The whole product, in one screen
proof.heading: One of them is wrong. <mark>Look who scored higher.</mark>
proof.lead: Two children, one question from a real lesson. Read both answers before the grades land.
proof.question: Why did Nelson Mandela ask South Africans to forgive?
proof.footnote: The grader is never told which option was correct. Tomas picked the wrong one and out-thought the room — so that is what his parents read about on Sunday.

a.name: Ariana, 9
a.text: Because he was a good person. I just knew it was that one.

b.name: Tomas, 10
b.pick: He was afraid of more fighting
b.text: I don't think he was scared for himself — 27 years in prison already happened, so what is left to be scared of? I think he was scared for the country. If everyone took revenge there would be another war, and then the 27 years were for nothing.

rooms.heading: Three rooms. All of them ask why.
rooms.lead: Short enough to fit a school night. None of them can be finished by tapping.

defend.title: Defend Your Answer
defend.blurb: Two questions per lesson ask your child to explain themselves. Skipping is always allowed and never costs anything — a child made to justify themselves stops explaining and starts performing.

daily.title: Fake or Real
daily.blurb: Two claims a day, one of them invented. Spotting the fake is instinct; naming what gave it away is the skill, and only the naming earns credit.
daily.previewA: Honey found in ancient tombs was still safe to eat.
daily.previewB: A goldfish can only remember things for three seconds.

tricks.title: Spot the Trick
tricks.blurb: A chart, headline or survey built to mislead — and the trick is genuinely in the data, never described in the caption. Name the technique.

ladder.heading: You cannot level up by <mark>doing more.</mark>
ladder.lead: Ranks are gated on the range of thinking a child shows and the quality of what they write — never on hours logged. We tested exactly that.
ladder.proofA: 500 activities, repeating one kind of thinking
ladder.proofB: 14 careful activities, five kinds of thinking

report.lead: The findings are computed in code from what your child actually wrote. The model is only allowed to phrase them — it never sees the raw attempts, and it never touches the quote.
report.headline: She stopped trusting the first answer.
report.summary: Maya wrote four explanations this week. Three of them questioned something the question had quietly assumed — including one where she talked herself out of an answer she had already given.
report.quoteQuestion: On: Why did people queue for a whole day to vote?
report.quote: It says they waited 12 hours but that is only the people who stayed. Nobody counted the ones who gave up and went home, so we do not actually know how many wanted to vote.
report.quoteNote: Copied exactly. Maya got this question wrong.
report.climbingBody: Three times this week, up from once last week.
report.nextBody: Ask her what this reminds her of. She has not linked two topics yet.
report.caption: Below three explanations we show no report at all. A thin report is worse than none.

dinner.heading: Three questions. No screen.
dinner.lead: Every report ends with three open questions tied to what your child actually explored that week.
dinner.q1: If nobody counted the people who gave up queuing, what else might we be getting wrong when we count things?
dinner.q2: Can you think of a time you changed your mind about something halfway through?
dinner.q3: What is something you waited a really long time for?
dinner.note: Ordered hardest to easiest, so a tired child still gets one they can answer.

promise.heading: What we will not do.
promise.lead: Every item here is somewhere the easier version of this business makes more money.

logins.title: No child accounts
logins.body: Children get no email and no password. Under-13s cannot meaningfully consent, so consent is recorded once — with you.

words.title: A child's writing is never edited
words.body: The attempts table has no update policy at all. Not by us, not by an admin, not by accident.

index.title: Nothing your child writes is indexed
index.body: Every page holding their words is disallowed in robots.txt and marked noindex.

thin.title: No report when there is nothing to say
thin.body: Under three explanations in a week you get a plain note saying so, not a padded page of encouragement.

sources.title: Every claim says where it came from
sources.body: A source note is required at the database level on every daily challenge. A game about checking claims cannot fail to cite its own.

close.sub: Create a parent account, add a child, play one lesson — and read what comes back.
close.note: Free to start. An email and a password, and that is the whole signup.

maths.hubLead: Adding, taking away, times tables, fractions and percentages — each one drawn, so you can see what the numbers are doing before you work out the answer.
maths.whyBody: Most children who say they cannot do maths can do the maths perfectly well — it is the notation that defeats them. A child who finds 3 x 4 meaningless has no trouble counting a tray of buns three rows deep. Every picture here is drawn from the numbers in the question, so it can never disagree with it.

addition.name: Adding
addition.blurb: Adding is moving forward along the line.
addition.idea: Every sum is a jump to the right. The answer is wherever you land.

a1.prompt: Start at 3 and jump forward 4. Where do you land?
a1.note: Adding always moves to the right. The size of the jump is the number you add.

a2.note: When the ticks go up in twos, count the jump in ones — the line is the same, only the labels changed.

a3.prompt: 9 + 6. Jump to 10 first, then do the rest. Where do you land?
a3.note: Jumping to the nearest ten first makes the second jump easy: 9 + 1 = 10, then 5 more.

a4.note: Start from the bigger number and the jump is shorter, so there is less to count.

subtraction.name: Taking away
subtraction.blurb: Taking away is moving back the other way.
subtraction.idea: Subtraction is the same line, walked backwards. The gap between two numbers is the difference.

s1.prompt: Start at 9 and jump back 4. Where do you land?
s1.note: Taking away always moves to the left. Same line, opposite direction.

s2.note: Jump back to 10 first, then take the rest: 15 − 5 = 10, then 3 more.

s3.prompt: 13 − 7. Count the gap from 7 up to 13 instead of jumping back.
s3.note: Subtraction is also the distance between two numbers, and counting up is often easier.

s4.note: The line does not stop at zero. Three steps past it is negative three.

multiplication.name: Times tables
multiplication.idea: Every times fact is a rectangle of dots. 3 x 4 and 4 x 3 are the same rectangle, turned.

m1.note: Rows times columns. You never have to count them one at a time.

m2.prompt: And now? Look carefully before you count.
m2.note: Turning the rectangle does not change how many dots there are. 3 x 4 = 4 x 3.

m3.note: Five of anything is half of ten of it: 6 x 10 = 60, so 6 x 5 = 30.

m4.note: Hard ones split: 7 x 4 is 5 x 4 plus 2 x 4, which is 20 + 8.

m5.prompt: 24 dots in 4 rows. How many in each row?
m5.note: Dividing asks the rectangle a question backwards: 24 split into 4 rows.

fractions.name: Fractions
fractions.blurb: A fraction is a whole thing, cut fairly.
fractions.idea: The bottom number says how many equal pieces. The top says how many you have.

f1.prompt: What fraction of the bar is shaded? Write it like 1/2.
f1.note: Four equal pieces, three of them shaded. The bottom number is always the number of pieces.

f2.prompt: What fraction is shaded? Write the simplest answer.
f2.note: 4 out of 8 is the same amount as 1 out of 2. The bar does not change, only the way you name it.

f3.prompt: Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? Write your answer like 1/3.
f3.note: More pieces means smaller pieces. Cutting a bar into four gives you less each time than cutting it into three.

f4.prompt: The whole bar is shaded. What is that as a whole number?
f4.note: When the top and the bottom match, you have the whole thing, and that is always 1.

f5.note: 3/6 and 1/2 cover the same length. Equivalent fractions look different and mean the same.

percentages.name: Percentages
percentages.blurb: Per cent just means out of a hundred.
percentages.idea: A percentage is a fraction with 100 underneath. The grid has 100 squares, so you can see it.

p1.prompt: What percentage of the grid is shaded? Write the number only.
p1.note: Per cent means out of a hundred. Twenty-five shaded squares is 25%.

p2.prompt: What fraction is this, in its simplest form? Write it like 1/2.
p2.note: 50% is half. Percentages and fractions are two names for the same picture.

p3.prompt: 10% of 100 is 10. So what is 10% of 50?
p3.note: 10% is always a tenth. To find it, divide by ten, whatever the number is.

p4.note: The whole grid is 100%. Whatever is left is 100 minus the shaded part.

p5.prompt: The whole bar is worth 20, split into 5 equal parts. What is one part worth?
p5.note: One fifth is 20%. Splitting into five equal parts and taking one is the same as finding 20%.
